meta.title: The AI Toolchain: Cowork, Codex & Madison

slides.title: The AI Toolchain: Cowork, Codex & Madison
slides.subtitle: Five roles, one pipeline, and the moment you realize architecture is brand.

slides.title: Same model. Opposite products.
slides.lead: Hand two teams the same frontier model — identical weights, identical API — and one builds Cursor, the other builds Devin.
bullets: The thing that made them different was not the model. It was **the architecture** — the choice of where to put the seams.
That choice is the central skill in AI product design, and it is almost never taught.
Most people have a vivid sense of what they want the thing to *do*, and no framework at all for how its internal structure decides how it fails.
We will use **Madison** — an open-source, agent-based marketing intelligence framework — as the specimen.

slides.title: "Agent" means four different things
slides.lead: In 2026 this one word carries at least four distinct meanings, and the speaker rarely signals which one they intend.
slides.why: chapter enumerates Meaning one through Meaning four, each with its own example product, architectural implication, and failure mode — a genuine two-level taxonomy under one word

slides.section: why the meaning decides the product
slides.title: Recoverable error, or silent disaster
slides.lead: The four meanings are not in conflict. They are different levels of abstraction — and meanings three and four produce completely different failure modes.
bullets: An autonomous system that hallucinates partway through a twelve-step task has **corrupted its own output by the time you notice**.
A role-in-pipeline that hallucinates at step three fails *loudly, immediately, at a known location*.
You can fix it. You can tell a customer exactly what broke.
The architecture is the difference between a recoverable error and a silent disaster.

slides.title: Five specialized roles, one coordinating layer
slides.lead: An agent is a role with a defined job. Five roles report into one orchestration layer — and Performance is the one that closes the feedback loop back into it.
slides.why: chapter names five specialized layers each with stated inputs and outputs, 'connected through a sixth coordinating layer' — a dependency chain, and Performance 'closes the feedback loop'

slides.title: Madison made the org chart machine-readable
slides.lead: If you are a working marketer, that list should feel familiar. A research team. A content team. An analytics function.
bullets: That borrowing is not accidental and it is not trivial. Organizations divided marketing this way because the functions have genuinely different information needs, cadences, and success metrics.
Intelligence needs fresh data every morning. Content needs a brief and brand guidelines. Performance needs experiment results and *statistical patience*.
Designing agents along the same boundaries means each can be optimized without knowing how the others work internally.
The orchestration layer handles the connective tissue.

slides.title: The mega-agent breaks in three places
slides.lead: Suppose you built Madison as a single large model with a long prompt and access to every data source. On a demo, this works. In production, three things break, in sequence.
slides.why: chapter states all three verdicts explicitly — token costs, blurred failure modes, no product surfaces — and says 'the layered design solves all three problems at once'; the reader's own pipeline is untested

slides.title: A named layer is a sales surface
slides.lead: "Our Intelligence layer is running correctly; our Content layer is returning off-brand output." That sentence encodes diagnostic capability.
bullets: It also encodes a **sales** capability. You can sell tiers. You can sell the Intelligence layer to a customer who does not yet need the Content layer.
You can version each layer independently. You can hire a vendor to replace one layer without rebuilding the system.
From the customer's side, a mega-agent is a black box: nothing to name, nothing to version, nothing to sell separately. **The architecture is also an invisibility trap.**
The engineering choice and the brand choice are the same choice.

slides.title: Two products, one technology, two theories of risk
slides.lead: A senior developer choosing between them is not comparing capability benchmarks. They are comparing models of agency and trust.
slides.why: the chapter's own opening claim is a divergence: 'the same frontier language model — identical weights, identical API' splitting on the architectural commitment into two brand positions

slides.title: ReAct: reasoning without reaching is just thinking
slides.lead: Yao et al., 2023. An LLM doing useful work in the world has to interleave two operations.
bullets: *Reasoning* — thinking in natural language about what to do next. *Acting* — calling a tool, querying an API, modifying state.
Pure chain-of-thought is all thinking, no reaching. Pure tool-use is reactive, with no plan threading the actions together.
Yao et al. showed a **34 percentage point** improvement over imitation learning on ALFWorld. That is not a marginal gain.
The same loop structure runs in every Madison layer, with different tools and different reasoning prompts.

slides.title: Thought → Action → Observation → Thought
slides.lead: The LLM is not just calling APIs. It is reasoning about *why* it is calling them and *what to do* with what comes back.
slides.why: chapter prints the loop as a cycle and its figure calls out 'the observation-to-thought feedback arrow that distinguishes a true agent loop from a plain prompt'

slides.title: The 7 a.m. news run
slides.lead: An Intelligence Agent reasoning its way through a morning news cycle for Brand X.
slides.why: the chapter prints the trace with its own stated counts — 870 articles received, 87 unique after deduplication, 87 returned with scores; nothing downstream of the dashboard is stated

stages.label: acted on by the other layers

slides.title: The dangerous failures are the quiet ones
slides.lead: Understanding the loop teaches you exactly where it fails — and each failure needs a different design response.
slides.why: chapter ranks them: a reasoning failure is 'expensive, recoverable'; a hallucinated action is 'far more dangerous because it is silent'; an observation failure is 'the most dangerous category'

rungs.label: Reasoning failure
rungs.note: scores all 870 without deduplicating first — add a guard

rungs.label: Action failure
rungs.note: the tool errors, or the model hallucinates success — make it loud

rungs.label: Observation failure
rungs.note: plausible-but-wrong result propagates downstream — Performance is what catches it

slides.title: Predictability or flexibility. Pick knowingly.
slides.lead: Two dominant patterns in production systems in 2026, and Madison's reference implementation picks one.
bullets: **Graph-based** — n8n, LangGraph. The workflow is a directed graph defined in advance. Every path is explicit, testable, auditable.
**Conversation-based** — Microsoft AutoGen. The orchestrator is a meta-agent talking to sub-agents; they self-organize on task sequences nobody pre-specified.
Madison chose predictability, because the operational question is not "can this handle a task I didn't anticipate?" It is "can this be trusted to run at 7 a.m. every day *without surprising anyone*?"
Flexibility is not free: the failure modes are harder to isolate and the debugging surface is enormous.

slides.title: Human-in-the-loop is risk engineering, not philosophy
slides.lead: Madison includes human validation as an explicit architectural feature, not an afterthought.
slides.why: chapter draws the boundary and names the three crossings by name — 'what content to publish, how to allocate campaign budget, what persona to deploy … are reviewed by a human before execution'

slides.title: McLuhan was right about your codebase
slides.lead: He argued the structure of a communication system carries its own meaning, independent of content. He could not have anticipated how precisely that applies to software architecture.
bullets: Neither Cursor's nor Devin's brand position was written in a marketing document first. Both **emerged from architectural commitments made for technical reasons**, whose brand implications became visible later.

That is how most product positioning actually works: engineers make choices, choices create affordances, affordances create experience, and marketing writes copy describing what the engineers already produced.
You are in the rare position of designing a product from scratch. You can run this process deliberately.
The window is narrow. It closes the moment you commit to a data model.

slides.section: what this deck does not tell you
slides.title: Every grey slot is a thing you have to run
slides.lead: The counts on the news-run slide are the chapter's own — 870 in, 87 after deduplication. Everything else stayed empty on purpose.
bullets: Whether *your* pipeline holds on token economics, fault location and product surfaces — **TO RUN**.
Which of your decisions are expensive and hard to reverse enough to deserve a human gate — **TO RUN**.
Madison is a reference architecture, not a template. Reading it well teaches you what to do. Copying it produces a worse Madison.

slides.title: Design the decomposition first. The code is implementation.
slides.lead: A multi-agent system is a theory of how a job should be decomposed, written in code. Pick one Madison layer, trace it end to end, and name the two decisions in your own pipeline that must stay human-gated.
